events.title: Casa Branca
events.text: Nagô women, by tradition led by Iyá Nassô, found the Ilê Axé Iyá Nassô Oká in Salvador, the oldest Candomblé house still active.

events.title: Malê revolt
events.text: Enslaved and freed Muslim Africans rise in Salvador; the crackdown falls on all African gatherings.

events.title: Casa das Minas
events.text: A deed in São Luís names Maria Jesuína, a Jeje priestess, as owner of the house of the voduns.

events.title: Gantois
events.text: Maria Júlia da Conceição Nazaré founds the Gantois house in Salvador.

events.title: Slave trade banned
events.text: The Atlantic slave trade to Brazil ends, but slavery itself goes on for thirty-eight more years.

events.title: Domingos Sodré arrested
events.text: Police in Salvador arrest the freed African diviner Domingos Sodré and seize his sacred objects.

events.title: Alhandra's Jurema
events.text: Inácio de Barros, later venerated as a Jurema master, receives the lands of the old Indigenous village of Alhandra.

events.title: Sítio de Pai Adão
events.text: The African priestess Tia Inês founds Recife's oldest Nagô house in Água Fria.

events.title: Batuque in the press
events.text: A Pelotas newspaper reports African drum ceremonies, early evidence of the Batuque.

events.title: The Golden Law
events.text: Slavery is abolished in Brazil, the last country in the Americas to do so.

events.title: The Penal Code
events.text: The Republic's new penal code makes 'magic and its spells' and spiritism crimes.

events.title: Mina reaches Belém
events.text: Mãe Josina, from Maranhão, founds the first Tambor de Mina house in Belém.

events.title: A secular republic
events.text: The first republican constitution separates church and state and promises freedom of worship.

events.title: Nina Rodrigues
events.text: The physician Nina Rodrigues begins the first study of Candomblé, treating it as pathology.

events.title: The cabula
events.text: The bishop of Espírito Santo describes the cabula, a Bantu-rooted rite seen as a forerunner of macumba.

events.title: Prince Custódio
events.text: Custódio Joaquim de Almeida, revered as an African prince, settles in Porto Alegre and protects the Batuque.

events.title: João do Rio
events.text: The journalist João do Rio describes the African houses and macumbas of Rio de Janeiro.

events.title: Umbanda is born
events.text: On 15 November, the young Zélio de Moraes receives the Caboclo of the Seven Crossroads at a séance in Niterói.

events.title: Opô Afonjá
events.text: Mãe Aninha founds the Ilê Axé Opô Afonjá in Salvador.

events.title: Quebra de Xangô
events.text: On the night of 1 February, an armed political league sacks and burns the terreiros of Maceió.

events.title: Pelo Telefone
events.text: Samba registered from the circle of Tia Ciata, a Bahian priestess of Rio's Praça Onze.

events.title: Mina in Porto Velho
events.text: Migrants from Maranhão open the Recreio de Yemanjá, Rondônia's first Mina house.

events.title: Pedrito's raids
events.text: Police chief Pedro Gordilho's cavalry breaks up Candomblé ceremonies in Salvador.

events.title: Umbanda in the south
events.text: A railway worker founds the Reino de São Jorge, the first Umbanda house of Rio Grande do Sul.

events.title: Mário de Andrade's catimbó
events.text: The modernist writer is initiated into catimbó near Natal and writes down its songs.

events.title: First Afro-Brazilian Congress
events.text: Gilberto Freyre and Ulysses Pernambucano bring scholars and priests together in Recife.

events.title: Second Afro-Brazilian Congress
events.text: Édison Carneiro's congress in Salvador gives priests a voice and calls for freedom of worship.

events.title: Xangôs closed
events.text: Under the Estado Novo, a police order shuts the terreiros of Pernambuco.

events.title: The police museum
events.text: Objects seized by Rio's police are listed as heritage under the name 'Black Magic Museum'.

events.title: Folklore mission
events.text: Mário de Andrade's researchers record catimbó, xangô and Mina music across the Northeast.

events.title: Umbanda congress
events.text: The First Congress of Umbanda Spiritism meets in Rio to codify the new religion.

events.title: Umbanda in Curitiba
events.text: The Templo Sol do Oriente is founded, bringing Umbanda to Paraná.

events.title: Freedom of worship
events.text: The novelist Jorge Amado, as a deputy, writes freedom of worship into the new constitution.

events.title: Joãozinho da Gomeia
events.text: The Angola-nation priest moves his house from Salvador to Duque de Caxias.

events.title: Mãe Malvina
events.text: Mãe Malvina opens Florianópolis's first Umbanda centre, with drums.

events.title: Umbanda federation
events.text: Umbanda's first federation is registered in São Paulo, letting terreiros register as civil associations.

events.title: Umbanda in Fortaleza
events.text: Mãe Júlia Condante registers the first Umbanda terreiro of Ceará.

events.title: Goiás federation
events.text: Umbanda centres of Goiânia found a state federation.

events.title: Mãe Menininha
events.text: A hymn to Gantois's high priestess becomes a national hit, sung by Bahia's stars.

events.title: Police licences end
events.text: Governor Roberto Santos frees Bahia's terreiros from registering with the police.

events.title: Against syncretism
events.text: Five high priestesses of Salvador declare that the orixás are not Catholic saints.

events.title: Casa Branca listed
events.text: The Casa Branca becomes the first terreiro protected as national heritage.

events.title: The Constitution
events.text: The new constitution declares freedom of belief inviolable and protects places of worship.

chartNote: Share of the area of modern Brazil, by the dominant documented Afro-Brazilian tradition of each present-day state. A simplification: most states held several traditions at once, persecution kept many houses out of the record, and 'none recorded' means no lasting house is documented. The vast Amazon states swing the shares; Acre counts from 1903.
